title: Design resource intelligence foundation
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:

The current resource monitor has useful trainer hooks and event emission, but the target direction is broader than resource monitoring alone. We want a resource intelligence system that can record observations, build reusable run profiles, and support explicit accounting records without guessing ownership from raw counter deltas.

Scope:
- preserve the small trainer-facing resource monitor hooks
- define first-class observation, profile, and accounting record concepts
- separate collection, event/schema construction, sinks, aggregation/profile building, and accounting inputs
- keep cheap runtime monitoring available while allowing richer diagnostic modes
- design accounting around explicit known facts such as parameter sizes, optimizer state, cache artifacts, worker processes, checkpoint artifacts, and scoped measurements
- avoid treating reports/profiles as a halfway goal; reports should be outputs of the target resource intelligence model

Non-goals:
- do not revive the previous phase-resource-accounting OpenSpec direction as authoritative
- do not infer component ownership from aggregate deltas alone
- do not add a grab bag of new counters before the record model and seams are clear
notes: First implementation slice added: introduced ResourceObservationRecord, ResourceProfileRecord, and ResourceAccountingRecord under library.logging.resource_monitor; routed current JSONL/metadata event construction through ResourceObservationRecord while preserving existing monitor behavior; documented the resource intelligence direction in docs_design/resource_intelligence_foundation.md. Focused tests: timeout 180 ./.venv-wsl/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/logging/test_resource_monitor_records.py tests/unit/logging/test_resource_monitor.py tests/unit/metadata/test_observability.py tests/unit/metadata/test_metadata_runtime.py -q

title: Audit determinism and define a strict reproducibility mode
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:

The active training path appears reproducible in some local areas when a seed is fixed, but it does not currently guarantee deterministic run behavior end-to-end. The default training seed is null, some randomness is intentionally mixed into epoch preparation and augmentation paths, and the active launcher does not appear to enforce a repo-wide strict deterministic mode for CUDA/PyTorch behavior.

Scope:
- audit the active config-driven training path for determinism and reproducibility behavior
- identify which parts are deterministic today with a fixed seed and which are still nondeterministic
- inspect seed ownership across training setup, epoch preparation, validation, dataloader behavior, augmentation, sample generation, and any CUDA/PyTorch backend toggles
- define what a strict deterministic mode should guarantee versus what should remain best-effort reproducibility
- propose the config/runtime shape for an explicit deterministic mode if the repo should support one
- capture known trade-offs such as performance penalties, unsupported kernels, or backend limitations

Non-goals:
- do not assume the repo should force deterministic behavior by default
- do not implement a broad determinism overhaul without first auditing the active path and defining the intended guarantees

Acceptance:
- we have a clear picture of current determinism behavior in the active training path
- the remaining gaps are separated into audit findings, concrete implementation tasks, and any design/UX decisions about an explicit deterministic mode

title: Design resource allocation provenance and causality model
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:

The current resource-monitor schema can report counters and timing windows, but it cannot honestly answer which component, helper, or runtime owner caused a memory jump. The capability investigation confirmed that this is a design problem, not a missing-field problem.

Scope:
- study the current resource monitor, runtime trace, startup estimates, and report/debug seams
- define what kinds of provenance or causality claims are realistic in this repo and which are not
- separate hard attribution, best-effort attribution, and purely observational reporting
- evaluate whether any future implementation should use explicit local instrumentation around known operations, phase/subphase attribution, or a separate provenance/debug model
- capture platform/runtime constraints that affect any attribution model (CUDA allocator limits, temporary workspaces, distributed/offload cases, etc.)

Non-goals:
- do not add ad hoc provenance fields to ResourceMonitorFacts
- do not implement a large instrumentation system without a settled design

Acceptance:
- we have a documented design direction for provenance/causality work
- future implementation can distinguish observational metrics from best-effort attribution without overstating certainty
close_reason: Created the spec-driven OpenSpec change at openspec/changes/resource-allocation-provenance/ with proposal, design, specs, and tasks, and updated the resource-visibility investigation note/roadmap references to point future provenance work at that dedicated design track.

- add focused tests for any new payload fields and markdown sections

- do not redesign the live resource-monitor event schema unless a missing raw input is proven necessary

Acceptance:

title: Decouple runtime phase tags from resource-phase semantics and refine remaining timing coverage
description:
The remaining timing follow-up is no longer just "startup stalls" in the old narrow sense. We now need one coherent issue for the next phase of observability cleanup: separating runtime phase identity from implying resource-monitor treatment, while also deciding where finer runtime detail is still useful.

Why this issue exists:
- the current phase-tag vocabulary still reads too much like a resource-phase vocabulary
- adding a new runtime phase currently tends to imply new resource/report/console surface area, even when we may only want a trace boundary
- several runtime areas are still modeled coarsely (`startup.runtime`, final save/final checkpoint helpers, and any future finer startup metadata breakdown), but those decisions should be made under a clearer phase-model contract rather than by blindly adding more resource-visible tags

Scope:
- review and clarify the contract between runtime phase tags and resource-monitor phases/summaries
- decide what should be canonical runtime phase identity versus what should be surfaced as resource-monitor/report/console detail
- identify the remaining runtime areas that still need finer boundaries once that contract is clearer, especially:
  - `startup.runtime`
  - `_save_final_state_if_enabled()`
  - `_save_final_checkpoint_artifacts()`
  - any future `startup.metadata.*` breakdown, but only if startup metadata becomes interesting again
- capture whether additional phase categories, filtering, or mapping layers are needed so phase tags do not automatically imply equal weight across all observability surfaces

Non-goals:
- do not reopen the validation/sampling redesign-gated work here
- do not treat detailed per-device/allocation-visibility work as part of this issue; that remains under `sd-scripts-83b`
- do not restore the old compatibility-heavy metadata path just to get more timing granularity

Acceptance:
- we have a clearer model for how runtime phase identity relates to resource-monitor visibility
- the remaining runtime/detail candidates are grouped under that model instead of scattered as ad hoc tag additions
- any next implementation slice can add or refine timing boundaries without reinforcing the current ambiguity between phase tags and resource tracking
notes: Originally opened for startup stall / training-prep visibility. That startup investigation has already paid off: startup metadata cost was reduced materially and the remaining follow-up is broader than the old title suggested. Keep this issue as the umbrella for the next runtime-phase-model cleanup, including startup.runtime / finalization timing boundaries and any future startup.metadata breakdown if it becomes worthwhile again.

title: Investigate detailed resource usage observability and allocation visibility
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:

The current resource monitor captures useful high-level counters, but there is still open follow-up around richer resource-usage visibility: devices, VRAM, CPU memory, virtual memory, and where/when usage is allocated over the lifetime of a run. This needs a focused investigation before deciding what should become first-class observability metadata versus report-only diagnostics.

Scope:
- inspect the current resource monitor, startup summaries, and benchmark report surfaces for what resource facts are already captured
- identify missing useful visibility around device memory, host memory, virtual memory, allocation ownership/timing, and component-level attribution
- evaluate what can be measured reliably during training versus what would require best-effort heuristics
- outline which facts belong in live observability metadata, which belong only in reports/debug snapshots, and which may require a later dedicated design
- note any platform/runtime constraints (CUDA, accelerate, deepspeed, distributed, WSL, etc.) that affect feasible resource accounting

Non-goals:
- do not commit to a large implementation up front
- do not redesign the current resource monitor unless the investigation clearly justifies a targeted follow-up

Acceptance:
- we have a clearer picture of what detailed resource usage visibility is feasible and useful in this repo
- the remaining implementation candidates are better separated into live metadata, report/debug output, and future exploratory work

title: Evaluate broader host-memory and distributed resource semantics
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:

The current live resource schema now covers CPU RSS, CPU VMS, and per-device GPU maps, but there is still open design follow-up around whether broader host-memory detail or more refined multi-device/distributed semantics are actually worth adding.

Scope:
- evaluate whether host-memory fields beyond RSS/VMS would provide meaningful signal on supported platforms
- inspect how current local vs all_visible device_scope semantics behave relative to future distributed/offload cases
- identify which possible additions remain cheap observational facts versus which would require mode-specific or ownership-specific modeling
- recommend whether to keep the current schema as-is, extend it modestly, or defer further expansion

Non-goals:
- do not add fields just because they exist in psutil or backend APIs
- do not redesign the current resource monitor unless a clear benefit is shown

Acceptance:
- we have a clearer recommendation on whether broader host-memory fields or richer multi-device/distributed semantics should become first-class follow-up work

title: Design mixed-resolution training support, including RF resolution-aware shift behavior
description:
Track support for true mixed-resolution training in the active training stack. The current data path already supports aspect-ratio bucketing around a single base resolution, but it does not expose an intentional mixed-scale training mode such as 90% of batches at 1024x1024 and 10% at 2048x2048.

This issue should investigate and design the repo-owned implementation shape for:
- config surface for selecting multiple training resolutions and their weights or scheduling policy
- manifest, bucketing, epoch-preparation, and dataloader changes needed for deliberate mixed-scale batches rather than only aspect-ratio buckets around one base area
- caching and validation implications for mixed-scale manifests
- objective/runtime implications for rectified flow, especially whether training-time shift values should vary by resolution or sequence length instead of using one global timestep.training_shift
- interaction with future Anima/DiT-style model-family work, where mixed-resolution training may be required or strongly preferred

The output of this issue should be a clear design and implementation plan, plus any follow-up beads needed for execution.

title: Add optimization metadata emitters

Keep runtime-only optimizer metadata out of artifact payloads unless a projection explicitly opts in.
acceptance_criteria: Central optimization metadata emitters consume optimizer plans/runtime facts and emit typed records/events; tests prove runtime-only metadata does not leak into generic optimizer payloads or checkpoint metadata; docs describe which optimization facts are internal, reportable, or exported.

title: Fence deprecated PEFT scripts after training metadata helper removal
description: Deprecated sd_peft.py and sdxl_peft_copy.py still reference the removed training_metadata helper. Decide whether to delete, hard-fail with a clear deprecation error, or minimally migrate them to the metadata backbone without reintroducing compatibility wrappers.
close_reason: Deprecated SD/SDXL PEFT script copies now parse as retired stubs, fail with active train.py preset guidance, no longer import removed training metadata helpers, and have focused smoke coverage plus lint/direct import verification.

title: Design metadata analytics and export formats

acceptance_criteria: Document which metadata records should export to JSON/debug versus analytics formats; define versioning/privacy boundaries; identify whether Parquet or another format is warranted; produce implementation follow-ups if the design is accepted.

title: Explore performance runtime configuration boundaries
description: Investigate the repo-wide performance configuration/runtime surface after the config work settles. Cover memory-efficient attention backends (xformers, SDPA, mem_eff_attn, diffusers_xformers), FP8/base-model casting, RamTorch/model wrapping, checkpoint/offload knobs, and how these relate to optimizer-side quantization versus adapter/PEFT target quantization. This is not necessarily the next topic; metadata and logging may remain higher priority. The goal is to identify which performance controls should be universal repo runtime policy, family-declared behavior, optimizer-owned behavior, or adapter-specific behavior, then split concrete implementation work into narrower follow-ups.
acceptance_criteria: Inventory active performance.* config fields and their runtime consumers; distinguish live code from deprecated/vendor/test-only paths; document boundaries for attention backend selection, FP8/base quantization, RamTorch/offload, optimizer quantization, and adapter quantized-target support; create smaller follow-up beads for any implementation-worthy cleanup.

Include config-surface guidance and focused coverage for the chosen rule.

title: Add first-class DyLoRA rank-resize export support
description: DyLoRA's main value is that a large-rank training run can later be resized to a smaller target rank. Implement that as a first-class repo-owned DyLoRA capability in the main code path rather than as a separate side helper: for example, a runtime/module/export option that can intentionally emit a lower-rank LoRA-style payload from a DyLoRA-trained adapter. Keep the behavior inside the active adapter/method ownership boundaries, define how the target rank is requested, and add focused coverage for prefix/block truncation behavior and exported artifact semantics.

title: Investigate BOFT FastBlockDiag optimization path
description: Investigate whether repo-owned BOFT would benefit from a performance-oriented block-diagonal assembly path similar to Hugging Face PEFT's FastBlockDiag CUDA extension. Evaluate portability, build complexity, fallback behavior, and whether a repo-owned implementation is justified.

acceptance_criteria: Compare current repo-owned OFT parameter count and checkpoint layout against an upper-triangle-only design.; Decide whether the memory/compute savings justify the extra reconstruction complexity for this repo.; If adopted, preserve or explicitly migrate repo-owned OFT checkpoint compatibility and document the decision in library/adapters/methods/peft/README.md and CHANGELOG.md as appropriate.
notes: Repo guidance: there is currently no meaningful backward-compatibility pressure for repo-owned OFT checkpoints or parameter layouts. Prefer the best native design for this repo first; if old/full-block import support is ever needed later, keep it as explicit compatibility helpers outside the core training pipeline rather than shaping the training/runtime design now. This should be treated as an immediate follow-up after the current OFT landing work, not as distant backlog.
